questions.question: Consider the max-flow problem of a directed network with a source node $s$ and the sink node $t$. Let $x_{ij}$ (respectively, $x_{ji}$) denote the amount of positive flow from node $i$ to node $j$ (respectively, from node $j$ to node $i$). Write the node balanced equations of a nodes $i$ and $j$ where $i, j \ne s$ and $i, j \ne t$. [4 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
For an intermediate node (not $s$, not $t$) everything that flows in must flow out (flow conservation).
Node $i$ (sum over all its neighbours $k$):
$$\sum_{k} x_{ik} - \sum_{k} x_{ki} = 0, \qquad i \ne s, t$$
Node $j$:
$$\sum_{k} x_{jk} - \sum_{k} x_{kj} = 0, \qquad j \ne s, t$$
Here $x_{ik}$ is the positive flow leaving $i$ along $(i,k)$ and $x_{ki}$ the positive flow entering $i$; the arc between $i$ and $j$ appears as $x_{ij}$ (out of $i$, into $j$) and $x_{ji}$ (out of $j$, into $i$). All flows also satisfy $0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$.
Equivalently with net flow $f(i,k) = x_{ik} - x_{ki}$: $\sum_k f(i,k) = 0$ and $\sum_k f(j,k) = 0$.

rubric.point: Node $i$: total outflow $\sum_k x_{ik}$ minus total inflow $\sum_k x_{ki}$ equals 0
Node $j$: $\sum_k x_{jk} - \sum_k x_{kj} = 0$ (same rule written for $j$)

questions.question: Suppose you are solving a network flow problem using the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm and at a particular iteration, the remaining capacity of the edge $(i, j)$ is $r_{ij}$ (respectively, $r_{ji}$ in $(j, i)$) and you send a feasible flow $f(i, j)$ along $(i, j)$ then show that $r_{ji} = r_{ji} + f(i, j)$ holds for the residual network. [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Residual capacity is the capacity still available in a direction. Sending $f(i,j)$ units along $(i,j)$ uses up that much of $(i,j)$:
$$r_{ij} \leftarrow r_{ij} - f(i,j) \ge 0.$$
Net flow is skew-symmetric: $f(j,i) = -f(i,j)$. Pushing $f(i,j)$ from $i$ to $j$ is the same as pushing $-f(i,j)$ from $j$ to $i$. Applying the same update rule to the arc $(j,i)$:
$$r_{ji} \leftarrow r_{ji} - f(j,i) = r_{ji} - (-f(i,j)) = r_{ji} + f(i,j).$$
Meaning: after sending flow along $(i,j)$ we can later send up to that much back from $j$ to $i$, which cancels (undoes) the earlier flow. This back-edge is what lets Ford–Fulkerson correct bad early choices.

rubric.point: States the forward update $r_{ij} = r_{ij} - f(i,j)$ (residual = remaining capacity)
Uses skew-symmetry $f(j,i) = -f(i,j)$
Derives $r_{ji} = r_{ji} - f(j,i) = r_{ji} + f(i,j)$ and explains it allows flow to be cancelled

questions.question: Given a set of items $S = \{1, 2, \cdots, n\}$ and $m$ proper subsets $S_j$ of $S$, $j = 1, 2, \cdots, m$. You wants to covers all items in $S$ by choosing a number of $S_j$ with minimum cost; the cost of choosing $S_j$ is $c_j$. Write down the mathematical model of the weighted set covering problem by defining decision variables for optimization. Describe the physical meaning of the constraint sets in the mathematical model. [3+2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Data: $a_{ij} = 1$ if item $i$ is in $S_j$, $a_{ij} = 0$ otherwise ($i = 1, \dots, n$; $j = 1, \dots, m$).
Decision variables: $x_j = 1$ if subset $S_j$ is chosen, $x_j = 0$ otherwise.
$$\min \sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j x_j$$
$$\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j=1}^{m} a_{ij} x_j \ge 1, \quad i = 1, \dots, n$$
$$x_j \in \{0, 1\}, \quad j = 1, \dots, m$$
Meaning: the objective is the total cost of the chosen subsets (minimise it). The constraint for item $i$ says that at least one chosen subset contains item $i$, i.e. every item of $S$ is covered at least once. $x_j \in \{0, 1\}$: each subset is either taken or not (no fractions of a subset).

rubric.point: Defines $x_j$ (1 if $S_j$ chosen, else 0) and the incidence data $a_{ij}$
Objective $\min \sum_j c_j x_j$
Covering constraints $\sum_j a_{ij} x_j \ge 1$ for every item $i$, with $x_j \in \{0,1\}$
Meaning of the covering constraints: every item is covered by at least one chosen subset
Meaning of the binary constraints / objective: a subset is chosen or not; minimise total cost

questions.question: Construct a directed graph network with $s$ and $t$ as the source and terminal node, respectively, and define an $(s - t)$ cut-$(A, B)$ together with the corresponding capacity of the cut, $\text{CAP}(A, B)$. [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Example network (capacities on the arcs): $s \to a$ (4), $s \to b$ (3), $a \to b$ (2), $b \to a$ (1), $a \to t$ (3), $b \to t$ (5).
An $s$–$t$ cut $(A, B)$ is a partition of the nodes into two disjoint sets with $s \in A$ and $t \in B$ ($A \cup B = V$, $A \cap B = \emptyset$). Removing the arcs from $A$ to $B$ leaves no path from $s$ to $t$. Example: $A = \{s, a\}$, $B = \{b, t\}$.
Capacity: the sum of the capacities of the arcs leaving $A$ (from $A$ to $B$); arcs from $B$ back to $A$ are not counted:
$$\text{CAP}(A, B) = \sum_{e \text{ out of } A} c_e = c_{sb} + c_{ab} + c_{at} = 3 + 2 + 3 = 8.$$
The arc $b \to a$ (1) goes from $B$ to $A$, so it is left out. (For this network the max flow is 7, which equals the minimum cut $A = \{s\}$: $4 + 3 = 7$; every flow is at most every cut capacity.)

rubric.point: A directed network with $s$, $t$ and arc capacities
Cut defined: partition $(A, B)$ of the nodes with $s \in A$, $t \in B$, disjoint
CAP(A, B) = sum of capacities of arcs from A to B only, computed for the example

questions.question: State one of the most important properties of the MST subgraph of a graph. Find the minimum spanning tree (MST) sub-graph by inspection of the undirected graph below in Fig. 1, where the distance or cost of various edges are $c_{12} = c_{13} = c_{24} = c_{34} = 1$, $c_{14} = 2$ and $c_{23} = 3$ [1 + 3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Property: the MST is a tree, so it connects all the vertices with no cycles (hence exactly $n - 1$ edges), and it has the minimum possible total edge weight of all spanning trees.
MST by inspection: there are 4 vertices, so the tree needs $4 - 1 = 3$ edges. The four edges of cost 1 form the cycle 1–2–4–3–1; any three of them connect all four vertices without a cycle. Take
$$T = \{(1,2), (1,3), (2,4)\}, \qquad \text{cost} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.$$
It is minimum because every spanning tree has 3 edges and every edge costs at least 1, so no tree can cost less than 3. The diagonals $(1,4)$ (cost 2) and $(2,3)$ (cost 3) are not used. (Kruskal gives the same: take the unit edges in turn and skip the one that would close the cycle.) Any other choice of three unit edges is an equally good MST.

rubric.point: One correct property: spans/connects all vertices, no cycles ($n-1$ edges), minimum total weight
Three edges of cost 1 chosen that connect all 4 vertices without a cycle
Total cost 3 stated, with a reason it is minimal (or that the diagonals are not used)

questions.question: Explain why there are $(n-1)!$ possible distinct routes (solutions) in a Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) with $n$ cities. How many solutions are there in the quadratic assignment problem with $n$ facilities and $n$ locations? Why? [2 + 2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Fix the home (starting) city: a tour is a cycle, so where it starts does not matter. The second city can then be any of the remaining $n - 1$ cities, the third any of the remaining $n - 2$, and so on until the last city is forced:
$$1 \times (n-1) \times (n-2) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1 = (n-1)!$$
Each order is a different route (this count treats a tour and its reverse as different, which is right for the asymmetric TSP; in the symmetric TSP they have the same length, so there are $\tfrac{1}{2}(n-1)!$ distinct tours).
QAP: there are $n!$ solutions. A solution assigns each of the $n$ facilities to a different location, i.e. it is a permutation $\phi \in S_n$ (facility $i$ goes to location $\phi(i)$). Facility 1 has $n$ choices of location, facility 2 has the remaining $n - 1$, …, facility $n$ gets the last one: $n(n-1)\cdots 1 = n!$. There is no rotation to divide out, because the locations are distinct places (unlike the cyclic order of a tour).

rubric.point: Fix the starting city (a tour is a cycle)
The remaining $n-1$ cities can be ordered in $(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 1 = (n-1)!$ ways
QAP has $n!$ solutions
Reason: each solution is a permutation (one-to-one assignment) of the $n$ facilities to the $n$ locations

questions.question: Define an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm of a minimization problem in combinatorial optimization. [3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $P$ be a minimisation problem with set of instances $\mathcal{I}$, and let $A$ be an algorithm that returns a feasible solution $A(I)$ for every instance $I \in \mathcal{I}$. $A$ is an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm ($\alpha \ge 1$) if it finds that feasible solution in polynomial time for every instance and
$$A(I) \le \alpha \cdot OPT(I) \quad \text{for all } I \in \mathcal{I},$$
where $OPT(I)$ is the optimal (minimum) value of instance $I$. So the answer is never worse than $\alpha$ times the optimum; the closer $\alpha$ is to 1, the better the guarantee.

rubric.point: Setting: minimisation problem $P$ with instances $\mathcal{I}$; $A$ returns a feasible solution $A(I)$ for every instance
Runs in polynomial time
$A(I) \le \alpha\, OPT(I)$ for all $I$, with $\alpha \ge 1$ and $OPT(I)$ the optimal value

questions.question:
Consider the 7 city symmetric TSP with a feasible tour $x = (1, 3, 2, 6, 7, 4, 5)$ where the 1st city is the starting city. Answer the following questions:
(i) Construct two 2-Opt neighbors of $x$. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
2-opt move: delete two non-adjacent edges $(c_i, c_{i+1})$ and $(c_j, c_{j+1})$ of the tour and reconnect with $(c_i, c_j)$ and $(c_{i+1}, c_{j+1})$; this reverses the cities in positions $i+1, \dots, j$. Positions (not city labels) of $x$: $c_1 = 1, c_2 = 3, c_3 = 2, c_4 = 6, c_5 = 7, c_6 = 4, c_7 = 5$ (city 1 stays first).
• $i = 1, j = 3$: remove (1,3) and (2,6), add (1,2) and (3,6), reverse "3, 2" → $x^{(1)} = (1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 4, 5)$.
• $i = 1, j = 4$: remove (1,3) and (6,7), add (1,6) and (3,7), reverse "3, 2, 6" → $x^{(2)} = (1, 6, 2, 3, 7, 4, 5)$.
(Others, e.g. $i = 2, j = 4$: $(1, 3, 6, 2, 7, 4, 5)$; $i = 2, j = 5$: $(1, 3, 7, 6, 2, 4, 5)$.)

rubric.point: First valid 2-opt neighbour (two edges removed, segment between them reversed, city 1 first)
Second, different valid 2-opt neighbour

questions.question:
Consider the 7 city symmetric TSP with a feasible tour $x = (1, 3, 2, 6, 7, 4, 5)$ where the 1st city is the starting city. Answer the following questions:
(ii) Construct an example of a sub-tour that may occur in the solution process. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Sub-tour: without the subtour elimination constraints, the degree constraints $\sum_{e \in \delta(i)} x_e = 2$ can be met by several separate cycles instead of one tour, e.g.
$$1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1 \quad\text{and}\quad 6 \to 7 \to 4 \to 5 \to 6.$$
Every city has degree 2, but nothing joins $\{1, 2, 3\}$ to $\{4, 5, 6, 7\}$, so it is not a tour. In the STSP a sub-tour needs at least 3 cities (2 cities would use the same undirected edge twice). It violates $\sum_{e \in E(S)} x_e \le |S| - 1$ for $S = \{1, 2, 3\}$ (3 edges > 2), which is how the model cuts it off.

rubric.point: A sub-tour example on the 7 cities: two or more disjoint cycles covering all cities, each of at least 3 cities
Explains why it is not a tour (degree constraints met but cities split into separate cycles; violates the subtour elimination constraint)
